beats.narration_text: Stage one taught me a lot of patterns, and I didn't memorise any of them. I asked six questions of every piece of code instead. What's created once? Who closes it? Who configures it? Who imports whom? What happens when it's down? And where does it run? The patterns fall out of the answers.
beats.new_visual_element: The six questions as a set

show.event: six question cards land, three across then three, in spoken order
note lands: the patterns are the answers

props.title: Six Questions
props.note: Ask them of every piece of code. The patterns are the answers.

beats.narration_text: Question one: what's created once, and what's created per request? The database engine is created once, at startup. But once means once per process. My first Dockerfile ran five workers, and each built its own pool of twenty connections. That's a hundred: exactly Postgres's default limit, before a single user shows up. So the extra workers went.
beats.new_visual_element: Q1 — five workers, five pools, one hundred connections

show.event: '--workers 5' fans into five workers, each with its own pool of 20
the pools converge on '100 Connections', which lights terracotta
'Postgres · default limit: 100' lands — the numbers match

props.title: Created Once, Per Process
props.note: Each worker runs startup again, so each builds its own pool.

beats.narration_text: Question two: who opens it, and who closes it? A database session opens for each request, and something has to close it. Not the endpoint; it would forget. Here, FastAPI does it. The code runs up to yield, hands the session over, and finishes the cleanup once the request is done. Skip that, and about twenty requests in, the pool is empty and everything hangs.
beats.new_visual_element: Q2 — the real session dependency; yield is the handoff

show.event: the real dependency file reveals line by line
'with … as session: / yield session' lights terracotta on 'up to yield'
note lands: pool of 20, nothing closing — request 21 waits

props.title: Who Closes It
props.note: Pool of 20, nothing closing sessions: request 21 waits forever.

beats.narration_text: Question three: who configures it, and who only uses it? One file holds the values. Compose reads it and hands the values to each container when it starts. Inside, one settings object reads them, and every other module only reads that. The image itself holds code and never secrets, because anyone who gets the image gets everything inside it.

show.event: the chain builds: .env → compose → container → settings → every module
'Settings · one config object' lights terracotta
note lands: the image holds code, never secrets

props.title: Configure Once
props.note: The image holds the code. Compose hands it the secrets at start.

beats.narration_text: Question four: who imports whom? The rule I kept: shared code — the config, the database layer, the models, the service clients — never imports FastAPI. So the pipeline scheduler can import the exact same code the API uses. It's also why I picked Airflow 3 over 2: the older version pins an older database library, and couldn't have imported any of this.
beats.new_visual_element: Q4 — API and pipelines share one codebase

show.event: API routes and Airflow DAGs both point into 'Shared Code'
'Shared Code · never imports FastAPI' lights terracotta
note lands: why Airflow 3 — SQLAlchemy 2 can import the same models

props.title: Who Imports Whom
props.note: Airflow 3, not 2: its SQLAlchemy 2 can import the same models.

beats.narration_text: Question five: what happens when it's down? That depends on who's asking. The health endpoint catches failures, because its whole job is to report them. A pipeline task does the opposite: it raises. Here, if the API says degraded, the task fails on purpose, so the scheduler can retry it and flag it. Same failure, opposite reaction, and both are right.
beats.new_visual_element: Q5 — the real DAG task raises on 'degraded'

show.event: the real DAG task reveals line by line
'if status != ok: raise RuntimeError' lights terracotta on 'it raises'
note lands: /health catches, a task raises

props.title: Catch Or Raise
props.note: /health catches, so it can report. A pipeline task raises, so it can be retried.

beats.narration_text: Question six: where does this code run? My settings say the database lives at localhost. On my Mac, that's true. Inside the API's container, localhost is the container itself, and there's no database in there. Containers find each other by service name, so compose overrides the address to postgres. Same code, different machine, different answer.
beats.new_visual_element: Q6 — localhost means two different places

show.event: top row: from my Mac → localhost:5432 → Postgres
bottom row: from the API container → postgres:5432 → Postgres
'postgres:5432 · the service name' lights terracotta on 'service name'

props.title: Where Does It Run
props.note: Inside a container, localhost is the container. Use the service name.

beats.narration_text: The same question caught a security hole. A port written the short way, like nine-two-hundred to nine-two-hundred, really means every network interface on the machine, including the Wi-Fi. On a café or campus network, anyone could have reached the search engine, which has no password locally. Binding every port to localhost keeps it on this Mac only.
beats.new_visual_element: Q6, again — every published port bound to this machine

show.event: the real grep output: every published port starts 127.0.0.1
the OpenSearch 9200 line lights terracotta on 'the search engine'
note lands: short form = every interface; 127.0.0.1 = this Mac

props.title: Bind To This Machine
props.note: "9200:9200" means every interface. "127.0.0.1:9200:9200" means this Mac.

beats.narration_text: Here's the payoff. Next stage, I'm writing the piece that fetches papers from arXiv. Before any code, the six answers. One HTTP client, reused. The pipeline task opens it and closes it. Its address and delay come from settings. It lives with the shared code, so no FastAPI. When arXiv is down, it raises and the scheduler retries. And it runs inside the scheduler's container. Most of the design is already done.
beats.new_visual_element: The next piece of code, answered before it is written

show.event: the same six cards return, now carrying answers for the arXiv fetcher
'What If It's Down? · raise, so Airflow retries' lights terracotta
note lands: six answers, zero lines of code yet

props.title: The Next Piece
props.note: Stage 2's arXiv fetcher: six answers, zero lines of code yet.

beats.narration_text: Where do the questions stop helping? On a fifty-line script, most of the answers are obvious, so don't build layers for it. They tell you what to check, not to add structure before something actually hurts. And they don't replace the docs. They tell you which page to open.

show.event: three limits land left to right in spoken order
'Before It Hurts · no layers yet' lights terracotta

props.title: When Not To
props.note: Build the simplest thing. Add structure when something hurts.

beats.narration_text: So: six questions, and every decision in stage one traces back to one of them. You don't need to remember the patterns. You need to remember to ask. Next time: the bugs that taught me these, one by one.
beats.new_visual_element: Verdict artifact page — the six answers

show.event: artifact page opens; verdict lines land in order
the 'Next' line lands last

artifactLines: Created once: count processes, not just objects.
Open and close: one owner cleans up — here, FastAPI after yield.
Configure once. Everything else only reads.
Shared code never imports the web framework.
When it's down: health checks catch, pipeline tasks raise.
Where it runs decides what localhost means.
Next: the bugs that taught these.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, with a piece of your own code underneath it. Here is a piece of code from my project below. Ask me these six questions about it, one at a time, and wait for my answer before the next. What is created once, and what per request? Who opens each resource, and who closes it? Who configures it, and who only uses it? Who imports whom? What happens when each dependency is down? Where does this code run? Don't answer them for me. When I'm done, tell me which of my answers worried you most. The point is that you answer. Claude asks, and the thinking stays yours.

props.code:
import httpx
from src.config import Settings

class OllamaClient:
    def __init__(self, settings: Settings):
        self.default_model = settings.ollama_default_model
        self._client = httpx.AsyncClient(
            base_url=settings.ollama_host, timeout=settings.ollama_timeout
        )

    async def close(self) -> None:
        await self._client.aclose()

    async def list_models(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> list[str]:
        kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {}
        if timeout is not None:
            kwargs["timeout"] = timeout

        response = await self._client.get("/api/tags", **kwargs)
        response.raise_for_status()
        return [model["name"] for model in response.json().get("models", [])]
